notes.title: Start here: an analytics dashboard and a history meant to be read
notes.body:
3buildanalytics is an analytics and admin dashboard: a backend computes KPIs and charts from tracked events, caches expensive reads in Redis, and generates CSV exports, some in a background queue (BullMQ). Different roles may see different metrics.

This pack draws on four documents. Read them in this order:

1. `fabledocs/README.md`: the onboarding pack and how it relates to the larger `docs/` curriculum.
2. `fabledocs/03-git-workflow.md`: how branches, commits and PRs are written here, and a closing section on what building the backlog actually found. Most questions come from this file.
3. `docs/SENIOR_ENGINEERING_DECISIONS.md`: six short design decisions, one paragraph each.
4. `docs/DEBUGGING_GUIDE.md`: symptom-first checklists.
5. `docs/upskill/03-architecture-and-patterns/04-side-effects-async-and-reliability.md`: a map of side effects and their reliability questions.

That last guide's line numbers point at an older version of `backend/src/modules/exports/exports.service.ts`. When it raises a question, open the current file: several of its concerns have since been fixed, and the comments in the code explain how.

excerpts.quote: The branch, commit, and PR conventions this repo models — with PR #1 as a worked example — plus current backlog status
This repo's history is meant to be *read*. Every branch, commit, and PR is written so that someone learning the codebase can follow not just what changed but why.

notes.title: Concept: commits and PRs as the record of reasoning
notes.body:
The workflow guide treats git history as documentation for the next engineer. A few habits follow from that:

- **One story, one branch, one PR.** The branch name carries the story id, so it explains itself months later.
- **Commits.** Read what the guide says a commit should be and what its message should explain, and then how that connects to the merge style the repo uses for PRs.
- **The PR body is for the reviewer.** It says why, what changed, which bugs were found, how to review, exactly what was verified, and what was deliberately left out.
- **Say what you did not verify.** A reviewer who knows the gap can weigh it.

The last section of the guide, "What the work actually found", is a list of real surprises found by building and testing rather than by reading the code. Read each one and ask what made the bug invisible until someone ran something.

excerpts.quote: This repo's history is meant to be *read*. Every branch, commit, and PR is written so that someone learning the codebase can follow not just what changed but why. This document explains the conventions so you can match them.

**Say what you did not verify.** That PR stated plainly that the Playwright spec had never been run locally because browsers were not installed, and that CI was the only place it executed. A reviewer who knows the gap can weigh it. A reviewer who is told "all tests pass" cannot.

readMore.why: The PR template and the two habits worth copying.

notes.title: Concept: exports, queues and side effects
notes.body:
A CSV export is a long-running job with several **side effects**: a database row for the job, a file on disk, tracked and audit events, and possibly a message on a Redis queue. The side-effects guide lists each one with the question a reviewer should ask: what if this step fails after the previous one succeeded?

The decisions document explains why exports are jobs at all: big CSV generation is slow and failure-prone, so it is safer as a background job than as one giant synchronous download.

When you read `exports.service.ts`, find three things:

- the row-count threshold that decides between processing a job immediately and handing it to the queue;
- how a job is retried, and whether a retry creates anything new;
- what processing does when the queue delivers the same job twice, or when the queue cannot be reached at all.

The code comments above `retry` and inside `processJob` explain the bugs these were written to fix.

excerpts.quote: Large CSV generation is long-running and failure-prone. Export jobs create a safer user experience and a clearer operational model than synchronous giant downloads.
| Side effect | Where triggered | Reliability question |

notes.title: A security control that did nothing
notes.body:
`metricVisibilityMiddleware` tried to stop ordinary users from forcing a full recomputation by changing `req.query` (removing or overriding `refresh=true`). But in Express, `req.query` is re-parsed from the URL, so assigning to it does not stick: the assignment was **silently discarded**. Nothing errored, and any user could still force a recomputation. US-16 found this by *testing* the control instead of reading it, and the guide says the commit that proves it is worth more than the fix.

Why the others are wrong:
- **everyone was blocked**: the problem is the opposite: nobody was blocked.
- **worked only with startDate**: no such condition is described; the assignment never had any effect.
- **threw a 500 on every request**: it failed silently, which is why it went unnoticed.

excerpts.quote: US-16 opened by *testing* whether `metricVisibilityMiddleware` restricted `?refresh=true`. It did not — Express re-parses `req.query`, so the assignment was discarded and any user could force full recomputation.

notes.title: Why this repo merges instead of squashing
notes.body:
Squash merging turns all the commits on a branch into one. That is fine when commits are checkpoints. Here, each commit is written as a chapter that a reader is meant to follow (PR #1 shipped seven), and the history is part of what the repo teaches. Squashing would collapse those chapters **into one blob**, destroying the thing the history exists for. So PRs are merged with `--merge` and the branch is deleted.

Why the others are wrong:
- **squash cannot delete the branch**: `--delete-branch` works with either strategy; it is not the reason.
- **squash breaks required CI checks**: the guide requires green CI either way; nothing says squash breaks it.
- **--merge gives linear history for bisect**: merge commits make history less linear, not more.

excerpts.quote: This repo merges with `--merge`, not `--squash`. Squashing would collapse those seven chapters into one blob and destroy exactly the thing this history exists to teach.

notes.title: Encode the follow-up in the test suite
notes.body:
The malformed-token 500 was a real bug, but outside the PR's scope. The PR did not hide it or patch it quietly. It committed an `it.skip` test describing the correct behaviour, assigned to US-04, and **also** a passing test that pins today's 500. The trick: when someone fixes the bug, the pinning test fails, which forces them to find and un-skip the real test. The guide's rule: encode the follow-up in the test suite, not in a TODO comment, because TODOs rot silently.

Why the others are wrong:
- **deleted the failing test**: the guide says neither defect was quietly deleted.
- **a TODO comment**: exactly what the guide warns against.
- **a quiet fix in the same PR**: the guide says neither was silently patched; it was out of scope.

excerpts.quote: They were committed as `it.skip` with an explanation and assigned to US-04 — and the 500 was additionally pinned by a *passing* test, so fixing it breaks that assertion and forces whoever does US-04 to un-skip its counterpart.
**encode the follow-up in the test suite, not in a TODO comment.** TODOs rot silently; a failing assertion does not.

notes.title: Graceful degradation that waited forever
notes.body:
A `try/catch` only helps if something throws. With `maxRetriesPerRequest: null`, ioredis does not fail a command when Redis is down; it **queues the command and waits**, forever. So no error ever reached the `catch`, and requests hung instead of falling back. The real commit message explains this, and notes that BullMQ was left alone because its blocking commands genuinely need that setting. The guide's lesson: bound the operation yourself; do not trust a library's timeout defaults.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Express skips try/catch in async handlers**: try/catch is plain JavaScript and works; it simply had nothing to catch.
- **BullMQ held a lock on the connection**: the cache client's own setting caused the wait.
- **the catch re-threw**: the catch never ran at all.

excerpts.quote: `maxRetriesPerRequest: null` made ioredis queue commands forever, that the surrounding try/catch therefore never ran
Both *waited* rather than failing, so the surrounding `try/catch` never ran. Lesson: bound the operation yourself; do not trust a library's timeout defaults.

notes.title: Hiding a page is not security
notes.body:
Hiding the revenue page in the navigation only changes what the menu shows. A Viewer can still call the API directly, or see the metric through another page. If they see a revenue metric, the server sent it. So the place to look is the **backend**: the permission middleware that decides who may call an endpoint, and the server-side filtering that decides which metrics go into a response. The debugging guide's checklist says exactly this, and adds: do not trust frontend navigation hiding as security.

Why the others are wrong:
- **frontend route guards**: those are also frontend; the data still came from the server.
- **seed data**: Viewers may legitimately exist alongside revenue data; the filter decides what they see.
- **cache TTL**: staleness could show old numbers, but a role seeing a metric it should never see is a permission problem first.

excerpts.quote: ## Role Sees Too Much - Verify backend permission middleware. - Verify server-side metric visibility filtering. - Do not trust frontend navigation hiding as security.

notes.title: Tests that skipped themselves and looked green
notes.body:
The rate-limit tests needed Redis, and they were written to skip if Redis was not reachable. In CI, the Redis client was created with `lazyConnect`, so it had not connected yet when the tests checked it; the first `ping()` failed and the tests **skipped themselves**. A skipped test is not a failure, so CI showed green while nothing was tested. The guide's lesson: tests that skip quietly are worse than tests that fail.

Why the others are wrong:
- **a mock Redis let everything through**: the problem was a skip, not a permissive mock.
- **limiter disabled in the CI env file**: no such setting is described; the cold client was the cause.
- **deliberately it.skip'd**: those were the auth tests; these skipped by accident.

excerpts.quote: US-18's rate-limit tests reported green in CI while doing nothing, because a cold `lazyConnect` client failed its first `ping()`. Tests that skip quietly are worse than tests that fail.

notes.title: Why the backend returns aggregates
notes.body:
The decisions document gives three reasons in one sentence: sending raw event rows and letting the browser compute the metrics is **slower** (far more data to transfer and process), **leakier** (every row reaches the browser, including details a role may not be allowed to see), and **harder to reason about** (each page would compute its own numbers, and they could disagree). Returning a trusted summary from the server keeps all three under control.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Redis caches only scalars**: Redis can store any serialized value; caching is not the reason.
- **the 10,000-row export limit**: that limit is for synchronous exports, not dashboard responses.
- **the chart library cannot group by date**: the document says nothing about the charting library.

excerpts.quote: ## Aggregates Over Raw Rows Dashboard consumers need trusted summaries. Returning raw rows and asking the frontend to compute metrics is slower, leakier, and harder to reason about.

notes.title: CI caught what the laptop could not
notes.body:
The test helper `resetDatabase()` truncated the database tables between tests but never cleared Redis. On the developer's laptop there was **no Redis at all**, so there was nothing stale to leak between tests, and US-12 passed. CI runs a real Redis, so cached data from one test survived into the next and US-12 failed. The guide draws the lesson: CI should run the real dependencies, because a laptop missing one can hide a whole class of bug.

Why the others are wrong:
- **parallel vs serial**: the guide names Redis, not test ordering.
- **CI clock in UTC**: not the cause given.
- **SQLite vs Postgres**: the difference that mattered was Redis being present, not the database engine.

excerpts.quote: US-12 passed locally and failed in CI: `resetDatabase()` truncated tables but never cleared Redis, and there is no Redis on the dev machine. An argument for CI running the real dependencies.

notes.title: A large export with Redis down falls back to synchronous
notes.body:
`dispatchJob` first estimates the row count. Up to `MAX_SYNC_EXPORT_ROWS` (10,000) it just processes the job immediately. 50,000 is above that, so it tries to add the job to the BullMQ queue. With Redis unreachable, `add` throws; the `catch` logs a warning, `export.queue.unavailable.falling_back`, and then **processes the job synchronously anyway**. The export still completes; it is just slower for the caller.

Why the others are wrong:
- **stays PENDING until Redis returns**: the fallback processes it now instead of waiting.
- **only up to 10,000 rows**: the fallback calls `processJob` on the whole job; nothing truncates it.
- **503 and the row deleted**: no such branch exists in `dispatchJob`.

if (rowCount <= MAX_SYNC_EXPORT_ROWS) { return exportsService.processJob(jobId, {

notes.title: The retry that leaked a pending job every time
notes.body:
The comment above `retry` tells the story. The old code set the failed job back to PENDING and then called `create()`, which inserted a **second** job. The new job ran; the original stayed PENDING forever, because nothing would ever pick it up. The engineering dashboard counts queue depth from PENDING rows, so every retry added one permanently-pending row and the backlog only went up. The fix reuses the same row and caps retries at `MAX_RETRIES` (3).

Why the others are wrong:
- **deleted completed jobs**: nothing was deleted; the leak was an extra row.
- **doubled the estimated row count**: row estimates do not affect the backlog count.
- **counted twice by a metrics gauge**: the comment says depth is counted from PENDING rows, and the leak was a real row.

excerpts.quote: The previous implementation reset this job to PENDING and then called * create(), which inserted a *second* job. The original stayed PENDING * forever because nothing would ever pick it up, so every retry leaked one * permanently-pending row
const MAX_RETRIES = 3;

notes.title: A conditional claim stops double processing
notes.body:
BullMQ can deliver the same job twice, and the synchronous path can race a worker. Without protection, one export would be processed twice: two CSVs, two tracked events, two audit rows. So `processJob` now **claims** the job with one atomic `updateMany`: set status to PROCESSING, but only where the status is still PENDING or FAILED. If another worker already claimed it, the update matches **zero rows**, so this call logs `already_claimed` and returns the existing job without doing the work again.

Why the others are wrong:
- **runs again but suppresses the audit row**: processing does not run again at all.
- **throws a 409**: it returns the job quietly; nothing is thrown.
- **waits, then writes a second CSV**: it does not wait, and avoiding a second CSV is the point.

excerpts.quote: Only PENDING or FAILED can be claimed, and the update is atomic — if it * touches zero rows someone else already has it, so we return their result * rather than duplicating the work.
if (claimed.count === 0) { logWarn("export.job.already_claimed", { exportJobId: job.id, status: job.status }); return exportsRepository.findById(job.id);
